rationale: A wins because it finds four real doors into the story without pretending the facts are stronger than they are. Its pricing angle, "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices," is the kind of sharp business-model read a founder can actually pitch. B has good instincts, but "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents a competitive displacement story before the evidence earns it. That is how a decent angle turns into a reporter's follow-up question with teeth.
gaps_in_A: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is a little too causal and cute; the update says customers can hold keys via AWS KMS, not that the bank pilots happened because of that concession.
"the prevailing belief: modern cloud collaboration tools treat offline as a legacy concern" needs outside proof before it becomes the spine of a contrarian pitch.
The sovereignty angle needs one external peg or named regulatory requirement; A asks for it, but without it this is still a launch-adjacent trend read.
gaps_in_B: "quietly testing Notion" invents tone. The update says the banks run pilots; it does not say quiet, stealthy, leaked, or reluctant.
"clearing bars historically reserved for purpose-built regulated-industry software" overstates the facts. Pilots are not clearance, adoption, or compliance blessing.
"Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents incumbents, replacement, and competitive threat without a single named vendor or displacement fact.
B misses two of the cleanest available angles: offline-first as an architectural reversal and no pricing change as a security-upsell/pricing story. Those are better than the padded incumbent angle.
